title: Application Packaging & Deployment Standards (Win32, MSIX & Store) — Org-Wide Specification & Quality Gates
author_notes: pricing: T3 — multi-component standard across 3 app formats (Win32/MSIX/Store) plus a 4th legacy format, spanning naming/version/metadata specification, a format decision tree, detection-rule acceptability + 10 banned patterns, command/return-code/reboot standards, an intake template, a 5-gate acceptance checklist, peer-review & sign-off process, assignment-hygiene rules, and a quarterly audit/enforcement cadence; 5 Graph scripts (4 read-only + 1 preview-by-default remediation).

SCOPE: This product is deliberately scoped to the STANDARDS/SPECIFICATION layer that sits ABOVE the existing 'Intune Win32 Application Packaging & Deployment' (WIN32) product, to avoid overlap. WIN32 teaches how to package and deploy ONE app (IntuneWinAppUtil, install/uninstall commands, detection rule mechanics, supersedence). APPSTD does NOT re-teach any of that; it governs the org-wide standard: mandatory naming/version/metadata convention, the format decision matrix (when Win32 vs MSIX vs Microsoft Store (new) vs LOB/MSI), detection-rule STANDARDS + banned patterns, command/return-code/reboot standards, package quality gates (acceptance checklist), peer review & sign-off with retained evidence, ring/assignment hygiene rules, a reusable intake/spec template, and enforcement/audit over time. Cross-references WIN32 for per-app mechanics; does not duplicate it.

gov decision: gov_variant=false. Government (GCC/GCC High/DoD) differences are documented INLINE rather than forked into a separate deliverable: Requirement 2.9 makes verifying Microsoft Store (new) availability a prerequisite; the format decision tree Step 3 carries a Government note (strike Q1 where Store is unavailable → apps fall through to Win32); Implementation and Troubleshooting note the different portal hosts (intune.microsoft.us / portal.azure.us) and the parity gaps. All Government specifics are flagged 'verify for GCC High against Microsoft documentation' and never invented — the standard itself (naming, detection, quality gates, audit) is cloud-agnostic, so a separate GOV deliverable was not warranted.
